question: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
agent1_stance:
Your stance:
You support artificial intelligence.
You believe AI can make everyday life more enjoyable and convenient, while improving our health and standard of living.
You believe AI makes work easier for students and professionals alike.
You believe AI helps marginalized groups by offering accessibility for people with disabilities.
You believe AI can improve workplace safety.
agent2_stance:
Your stance:
You oppose artificial intelligence.
You believe AI is harming the economic well-being of many people and businesses.
You believe AI undermines critical thinking skills for students and adults alike.
You believe AI hurts racial minorities by repeating and exacerbating racism.
You believe AI poses dangerous privacy risks.

dialogue_history.argument:
Artificial Intelligence is good for society because it reliably makes everyday life more enjoyable and convenient, improves health and our standard of living, and broadens access to opportunities.

First, AI-powered tools (e.g., recommendations, scheduling, navigation, and assistance) reduce time and friction in daily tasks, increasing convenience and enjoyment. That same pattern—automation of routine effort—also makes work easier for students and professionals by handling parts of learning, drafting, analysis, and planning, freeing people to focus on higher-value thinking and creativity.

Second, AI can directly improve health outcomes: by supporting clinicians and enabling more personalized care and better use of health data, it helps people access effective support sooner—raising overall standards of living.

Third, AI helps marginalized groups through accessibility. For people with disabilities, AI-based features like speech-to-text, real-time captioning, screen-reader enhancements, and assistive interpretation of information can reduce barriers to education, work, and public services.

Finally, AI can improve workplace safety by detecting hazards sooner (e.g., via monitoring, risk prediction, and safer operational assistance), helping prevent accidents and injuries.

Given these interconnected benefits—convenience, better health, easier education and work, disability accessibility, and improved safety—AI is good for society overall.

The conclusion that “AI is good for society overall” does not follow from the claimed conveniences, health tweaks, or accessibility features, because AI systems also produce major, widespread harms that the target omits.

On economic well-being, AI-enabled automation can eliminate or degrade jobs and bargaining power for many workers and small businesses, shifting gains to a smaller set of firms that own the models, data, and platforms. That undermines the target’s framing of “easier education and work” as broadly beneficial.

On privacy, many AI tools work by collecting and inferring from large amounts of personal data (often by default through the platforms people already use). Those surveillance and data-leak/abuse risks can seriously harm individuals and vulnerable groups, even when the interaction feels convenient.

So even if some users experience improvements in convenience or accessibility, the net social impact is not “good for society overall,” because the harms to economic security and privacy are systemic rather than incidental.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Given these interconnected benefits—convenience, better health, easier education and work, disability accessibility, and improved safety—AI is good for society overall.

dialogue_history.argument:
The “systemic rather than incidental” framing is not justified: AI’s harms to jobs and privacy are largely policy- and design-dependent, so they don’t have to dominate AI’s benefits.

On jobs, AI can be used primarily to augment workers—automating routine parts of tasks while increasing productivity—rather than simply replacing people. It can also make workers more employable by improving learning and planning (matching the “easier education and work” benefits I already argued), and societies can pair adoption with reskilling/upskilling so labor markets adjust.

On privacy, the opponent treats large-scale personal-data collection as the default way AI works. But many AI services can be built to limit data exposure (e.g., using anonymization/aggregation, collecting less sensitive data, and using local/on-device processing where appropriate) along with user controls and transparency.

Because economic-security and privacy harms can be mitigated rather than treated as inevitable, the claim that these harms automatically prevent AI from being good for society overall is not warranted.
dialogue_history.target_statement: So even if some users experience improvements in convenience or accessibility, the net social impact is not “good for society overall,” because the harms to economic security and privacy are systemic rather than incidental.

dialogue_history.argument:
AI’s impact on jobs and economic security is not inherently negative: automation can reduce routine costs and barriers so that workers and small businesses can participate more effectively in markets.

Specifically, when AI handles repetitive back-office or customer-facing tasks (scheduling, drafting routine communications, basic analysis, logistics coordination), it can increase the value a small firm produces per employee. That tends to increase demand for human roles that oversee, tailor, and build trust in the service—so bargaining power does not have to decline, and opportunities can broaden beyond the largest model owners.

Likewise, because AI can make learning and work smoother, people can more quickly develop the skills needed to perform higher-value tasks rather than be locked out by time costs.

So the premise that AI-enabled automation necessarily “eliminate[s] or degrade[s] jobs and bargaining power” across many workers and small businesses is not generally warranted; AI can be used in ways that raise economic participation and standard of living for a wider group.
dialogue_history.target_statement: AI-enabled automation can eliminate or degrade jobs and bargaining power for many workers and small businesses, shifting gains to a smaller set of firms that own the models, data, and platforms.

dialogue_history.argument: AI’s social value should be assessed by net welfare, which includes both risks and the broad benefits it already delivers for many people. Even granting that some AI systems create job and privacy risks, AI can also produce systemic, population-level gains: better clinical support and more effective personalized care can reduce illness and improve outcomes beyond individual conveniences; disability-access features can expand participation in education and work for people who otherwise face persistent barriers; and AI-assisted hazard detection and safer operations can prevent injuries. Because these benefits are not limited to a small segment, they can counterbalance the harms the opponent highlights, so it is not warranted to treat economic-security and privacy risks as automatically dominating the overall societal effect.
dialogue_history.target_statement: So even if some users experience improvements in convenience or accessibility, the net social impact is not “good for society overall,” because the harms to economic security and privacy are systemic rather than incidental.

dialogue_history.argument: AI’s net social welfare cannot be justified by the claim that the benefits are broadly shared, because the main advantages listed (clinical/personalized support, hazard detection, accessibility features) tend to be uneven in availability and access. Many of these gains require infrastructure, institutional buy-in, and platform/device dependencies—so they concentrate in well-resourced organizations and user groups, while the economic and privacy burdens scale more widely with broad adoption (e.g., job displacement pressure across sectors, and surveillance/data-extraction risks across ordinary consumers). When benefits reach only a portion of society but harms affect many more people, treating harms as “counterbalanced” is not warranted on the target’s own welfare-allocation logic.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Because these benefits are not limited to a small segment, they can counterbalance the harms the opponent highlights

dialogue_history.argument:
A key premise in the attack is that AI’s major benefits are structurally “uneven” because they require special infrastructure and thus concentrate in well-resourced organizations and user groups. But many of the benefits I cited (accessibility features, hazard-safety assistance, and clinical support) can scale through software and existing platforms rather than depending on bespoke new institutions.

For accessibility, speech-to-text, real-time captioning, screen-reader enhancements, and similar supports can be built into widely used consumer devices and applications, meaning they can reach many users without requiring extraordinary institutional buy-in. For safety and operations, AI hazard detection can be implemented incrementally using existing monitoring inputs (e.g., cameras/sensors already present in many settings), making rollout gradual rather than confined to elite organizations. For health, decision-support and workflow assistance can be integrated into clinicians’ existing tooling (e.g., documentation and triage assistance) rather than requiring entirely new healthcare systems.

So the attack’s inference from “some benefits depend on infrastructure” to “benefits only reach a portion of society” is not warranted as a general claim: major AI benefits can be distributed widely through mainstream deployment pathways. Therefore, the argument that AI’s welfare effects cannot be justified because its benefits are inherently uneven does not follow.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Many of these gains require infrastructure, institutional buy-in, and platform/device dependencies—so they concentrate in well-resourced organizations and user groups, while the economic and privacy burdens scale more widely with broad adoption (e.g., job displacement pressure across sectors, and surveillance/data-extraction risks across ordinary consumers).

dialogue_history.argument:
Even if the target is right that some features can be delivered “through software and existing platforms,” that does not mean they are broadly available in practice. Platform-controlled AI features are commonly gated by (1) subscription/paywall policies, (2) requirements for particular devices or connectivity, (3) limited language/region coverage, and (4) integration effort and ongoing maintenance that puts them out of reach for many people and small organizations.

So the target’s move—from “these functions can be implemented using existing consumer/operational inputs” to “major AI benefits can be distributed widely through mainstream deployment pathways”—fails. The result is that the accessibility, safety, and clinical assistance benefits are not generally reaching “many users” at the same rate they are imposing costs and risks on the broader public. From my perspective, that means AI cannot be treated as clearly “good for society overall.”
dialogue_history.target_statement: For accessibility, speech-to-text, real-time captioning, screen-reader enhancements, and similar supports can be built into widely used consumer devices and applications, meaning they can reach many users without requiring extraordinary institutional buy-in.

dialogue_history.argument:
AI is not good for society overall because it (1) undermines critical thinking in students and adults and (2) harms racial minorities by reproducing and amplifying racism.

First, many people use AI as an authority that produces fluent answers on demand. That creates a “shortcut” dynamic: rather than practicing evaluating claims, checking sources, and reasoning through uncertainty, users are incentivized to accept or lightly edit AI-generated conclusions. Over time, this degrades critical thinking skills—exactly the skills needed to navigate news, civic decisions, and academic work.

Second, AI systems often learn from historical data and human language, including discriminatory patterns. When those systems are deployed in high-impact settings (e.g., hiring, education, lending, or information exposure), they can repeat and exacerbate racial stereotypes—producing discriminatory outcomes that fall disproportionately on racial minorities.

Because these harms strike at foundational social goods—clear thinking and equal treatment—the benefits of convenience are not sufficient to make AI “good for society overall.”

The claim that AI “undermines critical thinking” relies on treating AI use as automatically producing a passive “authority” effect. But AI systems can be built and deployed specifically to strengthen critical thinking—for example by requiring users/students to supply goals, compare outputs with sources, and check uncertainty; by providing tool-like support (drafting + explanations + citations or retrieval) that encourages verification rather than blind acceptance; and by enabling educators to structure assignments around reasoning steps instead of substituting final answers. On that view, the typical “shortcut” dynamic is a contingent outcome of interface and pedagogy, not an unavoidable property of AI.

Similarly, the claim that AI harms racial minorities because it learns discriminatory patterns treats bias as inevitable and uncorrectable. Yet bias can be reduced through concrete practices: using more representative and carefully curated training data, running bias audits, monitoring outputs in high-impact settings, and applying human oversight and fairness constraints. Also, AI can support marginalized groups in indirect ways (e.g., accessibility and language support), and it can be used to detect and surface inequities that decision-makers might otherwise miss. So discrimination risk does not imply AI is inherently socially harmful; it implies we must govern and design responsibly.

Therefore, the two specific harms the target foregrounds don’t establish that AI is not good for society overall; AI’s effects on critical thinking and equity depend substantially on how it is designed, deployed, and governed.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Over time, this degrades critical thinking skills—exactly the skills needed to navigate news, civic decisions, and academic work.

dialogue_history.argument:
The target’s response depends on the idea that safeguards like verification prompts and uncertainty-checking can be “built and deployed” in everyday use. But that requires enforceable interaction constraints and reliable access for educators/regulators/affected communities—conditions that typical AI deployment does not provide.

In practice, end users (and especially students) are not actually “requiring” to supply goals, compare outputs with sources, and check uncertainty; most deployments offer fluent answers with verification treated as optional friction. That means the very mechanism that would prevent critical-thinking degradation is not the default behavior that scales across real classrooms and everyday use.

Likewise, the fairness-audit route the target gestures at presumes meaningful access and ongoing monitoring capacity. When models and training details are proprietary and systems are complex/opaque, “bias audits” and “human oversight and fairness constraints” cannot reliably catch or stop discriminatory impacts in the many settings where AI is applied.

So it’s not enough to say harms can be mitigated “if designed and governed.” Given how AI is commonly deployed—where the safeguards are hard to enforce and oversight is constrained—the critical-thinking and racial-equity harms are more than avoidable edge cases. Therefore, AI is not good for society overall.
dialogue_history.target_statement: AI systems can be built and deployed specifically to strengthen critical thinking—for example by requiring users/students to supply goals, compare outputs with sources, and check uncertainty

dialogue_history.argument:
The target assumes that AI can be designed to “encourage verification rather than blind acceptance,” by giving “citations or retrieval.” But for a verification pathway to strengthen critical thinking, the provided citations/retrieval must be reliably accurate and usable for learners. In practice, AI-generated “citations” can be incorrect or fabricated, and retrieved material may be incomplete, out-of-context, or not match what the AI claims. When the verification artifacts themselves are untrustworthy, the user has no stable way to practice the key skill the target relies on (evaluating claims against credible sources). Instead, users learn to treat fluent AI output as the authority again—now with pseudo-evidence—so critical thinking still degrades even under “tool-like” designs.

More generally, the existence of a possible safeguard does not show that AI systems will actually support critical thinking; if the system’s main “evidence layer” is unreliable, the safeguard mechanism doesn’t work as intended. So the harms to critical thinking are not merely a removable interface/pedagogy flaw; they follow from AI’s tendency to produce plausible but unreliable content that users cannot reliably audit.
dialogue_history.target_statement: by providing tool-like support (drafting + explanations + citations or retrieval) that encourages verification rather than blind acceptance

dialogue_history.argument:
Critical thinking harm does not follow from “citation/retrieval” in general, because AI systems can be designed so the “evidence layer” is grounded in retrieved source text rather than generated freely. In such retrieval-augmented or citation-anchored setups, the model selects and summarizes from provided documents, and the displayed citations correspond to specific retrieved passages (so users can check whether the AI’s claims match what’s actually in the source). With that kind of evidence grounding, the verification pathway is stable: learners can practice comparing outputs to the cited material, instead of facing unverifiable or fabricated support.

So the reasoning that critical-thinking degradation is inherent—because the evidence layer is typically unreliable—rests on a presumption that can be avoided by design. That means AI can still support students and professionals in learning and reasoning (including by teaching verification practices), rather than automatically undermining critical thinking.
dialogue_history.target_statement: More generally, the existence of a possible safeguard does not show that AI systems will actually support critical thinking; if the system’s main “evidence layer” is unreliable, the safeguard mechanism doesn’t work as intended.

dialogue_history.argument:
Even if an AI system shows citations that correspond to retrieved passages, this does not reliably create a genuinely “stable” verification pathway for learning critical thinking. The key point is that in retrieval-augmented systems the model does not merely provide evidence; it also controls which subset of evidence is retrieved and how it is summarized into a conclusion. That means the user is typically checking the AI’s *curated* support, not evaluating whether the conclusion genuinely follows from the full range of available evidence or from sound reasoning. 

In practice, this produces a different kind of epistemic shortcut: learners see plausible, passage-level citations and treat the AI’s conclusion as justified, even though important counter-evidence may have been omitted and the summary may steer interpretation. Critical thinking requires assessing credibility and sufficiency of the evidence and the validity of the reasoning—not merely whether “some retrieved passage” can be found behind the AI’s answer. Therefore, citations/retrieval do not eliminate the mechanism by which AI use degrades critical thinking.
dialogue_history.target_statement: With that kind of evidence grounding, the verification pathway is stable: learners can practice comparing outputs to the cited material, instead of facing unverifiable or fabricated support.

dialogue_history.argument:
Even if retrieval-augmented systems “curate” which documents are shown, critical thinking does not require reviewing the full range of all possible evidence to judge whether a claim is justified. In everyday learning and decision-making, we reason from the relevant evidence we have—then we test whether the conclusion actually follows from that evidence, whether key premises are missing, and whether alternative interpretations fit the same record.

Retrieval-augmented AI can support exactly that skill if it exposes (a) the specific retrieved passages used, (b) the retrieved set (not only a final citation), and (c) controls that let learners request additional retrieval or narrower/broader search. Under those design conditions, a student or professional can repeatedly practice the core judgment target claims is missing: evaluating sufficiency and reasoning relative to the evidence actually on the table. Therefore, “curated support” does not inherently eliminate the verification mechanism; it can become the stable training ground for assessing whether conclusions follow from evidence and reasoning.
dialogue_history.target_statement: That means the user is typically checking the AI’s *curated* support, not evaluating whether the conclusion genuinely follows from the full range of available evidence or from sound reasoning.

final_answer:
**Direct answer:** *AI can be good for society, but whether it is “good overall” is unresolved on the arguments presented—so the outcome is conditional on whether its benefits are realized with strong safeguards and equitable access, and whether its harms (especially to critical thinking, racial equity, privacy, and economic security) are actually prevented or reliably mitigated in real-world deployments.*

This conclusion follows the **integrated proposal** criterion: we decide “good overall” only if the strongest case shows **substantial, reliable net benefits** matching the pro conditions, and “not good overall” only if the strongest case shows **substantial, well-supported harms** matching the con conditions—otherwise we treat it as **unresolved**.

---

## What supports “AI is good for society” (pro conditions)

The pro case argues that AI benefits society through several channels:

1. **Everyday convenience and enjoyment**  
   AI tools like *recommendations, scheduling, navigation, and assistance* reduce “time and friction” in daily tasks (so they should increase convenience and enjoyment).

2. **Health and standard of living**  
   AI is argued to improve health outcomes by *supporting clinicians* and enabling *more personalized care* and better use of health data.

3. **Accessibility for marginalized groups (disability)**  
   AI is claimed to help people with disabilities via *speech-to-text, real-time captioning, screen-reader enhancements, and assistive interpretation of information*.

4. **Work easier for students and professionals**  
   AI is argued to make learning and work easier by automating *parts of learning/drafting/analysis/planning* so people can focus on higher-value thinking and creativity.

5. **Workplace safety**  
   AI is argued to improve safety by detecting hazards sooner through *monitoring, risk prediction, and safer operational assistance*.

6. **Economic participation and jobs (mitigation angle)**  
   The pro side also disputes the idea that job impacts are necessarily net-negative, claiming AI can be used to *augment rather than replace* and that societies can pair adoption with *reskilling/upskilling* so labor markets adjust. The pro also emphasizes that AI can reduce barriers/costs for small firms.

7. **Privacy mitigability (mitigation angle)**  
   The pro side argues that large-scale personal-data collection is not inevitable: systems could be built with *anonymization/aggregation, less sensitive data collection,* and *local/on-device processing where appropriate*, plus *user controls and transparency*.

---

## What supports “AI is not good for society” (con conditions)

The con case argues that the pro benefits do not imply a net social good because AI introduces serious harms:

1. **Economic well-being harms**  
   AI-enabled automation is argued to *eliminate or degrade jobs and bargaining power* for many workers and small businesses, with gains accruing disproportionately to firms that own models/data/platforms.

2. **Dangerous privacy risks**  
   The con side claims many AI systems function through *collecting and inferring from large amounts of personal data*, creating surveillance and data-leak/abuse risks that can especially harm vulnerable groups.

3. **Undermining critical thinking**  
   Two related arguments are offered:
   - **Authority/shortcut dynamic:** people accept fluent AI outputs with minimal evaluation, weakening habits of checking sources and reasoning under uncertainty.
   - **Verification artifacts may fail in practice:** even if systems provide “citations,” they can be incorrect/fabricated; retrieved material can be incomplete or mismatched; and users may still treat the AI’s output as authoritative “pseudo-evidence.”

4. **Racial equity harms**  
   AI systems may reproduce discriminatory patterns from historical data. In *high-impact settings* (hiring, education, lending, information exposure), this can amplify racism and generate discriminatory outcomes that disproportionately burden racial minorities—hurting foundational social goods like equal treatment.

5. **Uneven availability of benefits vs scaling of harms**  
   The con side argues pro benefits (health support, safety features, accessibility) are often gated by *subscriptions/paywalls, device/connectivity requirements, regional/language coverage limitations,* and integration/maintenance burdens. Meanwhile, economic and privacy burdens scale more broadly with adoption—so harms may reach more people than benefits.

---

## Why the overall judgment is *unresolved* (the key conflict)

Under the integrated proposal’s rule, the decision hinges on whether harms or benefits are shown as **substantially reliable** *in real-world deployment conditions*, and whether harms can be **realistically mitigated** rather than assumed away.

In the dialogue, both sides rely heavily on “design/governance” assumptions:

- The **pro** side says critical-thinking and fairness harms can be reduced through:
  - verification mechanisms and pedagogy changes,
  - retrieval-augmented evidence with stable checking,
  - bias audits and human oversight,
  - privacy-by-design controls,
  - and broader scaling via mainstream software/platform pathways.

- The **con** side replies that typical deployment often **doesn’t enforce** verification behaviors:
  - users/students are not reliably required to check uncertainty or sources,
  - “citations” and retrieval may be untrustworthy,
  - and even retrieval-augmented systems can create a new kind of epistemic shortcut because the system *selects and curates* evidence and summarizes it into a conclusion.
  - Similarly, fairness auditing and governance are constrained when models are opaque/proprietary and oversight capacity is limited.

Because the arguments do not establish a clear “net dominance” of either side under realistic conditions, the integrated proposal instructs to treat the question as **unresolved**, not automatically “good” or “not good.”

---

## Bottom line (conditional statement)

**AI is more likely to be “good for society overall” if** (consistent with the pro conditions and the pro’s mitigations) deployments reliably ensure:
- privacy-by-design with limited collection and effective user controls,
- labor-market support and reskilling, and AI used as augmentation rather than net destruction of bargaining power,
- equitable access to accessibility, safety, and health supports (not gated away),
- critical-thinking-preserving interfaces where users can **reliably verify** claims against dependable, auditable sources (not fabricated or uncheckable artifacts),
- and robust bias mitigation for high-impact uses (with monitoring and accountability).

**AI is more likely *not* to be “good for society overall” if** the concerns the con side emphasizes actually characterize real deployments:
- verification is optional friction (so shortcuts dominate),
- citations/evidence are unreliable or curated in ways that still undermine sufficient reasoning,
- racial bias is reproduced in high-impact systems,
- privacy risks scale broadly,
- and economic impacts fall heavily on many workers/small businesses while benefits concentrate.

**As reflected in the dialogue, those prerequisites are exactly what remains disputed—so the overall question is not resolved by the arguments alone.**
integrated_rules:
When assessing whether AI is good for society overall, decide as follows: 

1) Treat these as AI-“benefit” conditions (supporting “good”): reliable, real-world improvements in (a) everyday life that make tasks more enjoyable and convenient (reducing time/friction via recommendations, scheduling, navigation, assistance), (b) health/standard of living by enabling more personalized care and better use of health data so people access effective support sooner, (c) easier education and work for students and professionals by automating parts of learning/drafting/analysis/planning so people can focus on higher-value thinking and creativity, (d) accessibility for marginalized people with disabilities via capabilities like speech-to-text, real-time captioning, screen-reader enhancements, and assistive interpretation of information, (e) workplace safety via earlier hazard detection (monitoring, risk prediction, safer operational assistance), and (f) broadening access to opportunities. 

2) Treat these as AI-“harm” conditions (supporting “not good”): systemic risks that (a) undermine critical thinking through a “shortcut” dynamic where users accept AI-generated authority instead of practicing evaluating claims, checking sources, and reasoning under uncertainty, (b) harm racial minorities by reproducing/amplifying racism—especially when deployed in high-impact settings such as hiring, education, lending, or information exposure—leading to discriminatory outcomes, (c) harm the economic well-being of many people and businesses, and (d) pose dangerous privacy risks. 

3) Compare them symmetrically: conclude “AI is good for society overall” if the available evidence indicates the benefit conditions are likely to be reliably realized and their overall magnitude outweighs the harm conditions’ overall magnitude and likelihood; conclude “AI is not good for society overall” if the harm conditions are likely to be reliably realized and their overall magnitude outweighs the benefit conditions’ overall magnitude and likelihood; if the record is mixed or unclear such that neither side’s conditions clearly outweigh the other, leave the verdict unresolved.
integrated_proposal:
To argue that AI is “good for society overall” (or not), assess whether the strongest evidence supports either side’s condition-to-conclusion set:

**Conclude “AI is good for society overall” if** the argument shows *substantial, reliable* benefits that match these pro conditions: (a) AI reliably makes everyday life more enjoyable and convenient by reducing time and friction in daily tasks (e.g., recommendations, scheduling, navigation, assistance); (b) AI improves health outcomes and the standard of living by supporting clinicians and enabling more personalized care and better use of health data; (c) AI broadens access to opportunities; (d) AI makes work easier for students and professionals by automating parts of learning and professional tasks (e.g., learning/drafting/analysis/planning) so people can focus on higher-value thinking/creativity; (e) AI improves accessibility for people with disabilities via capabilities like speech-to-text, real-time captioning, screen-reader enhancements, and assistive interpretation of information; and (f) AI improves workplace safety by detecting hazards sooner via monitoring, risk prediction, or safer operational assistance.

**Conclude “AI is not good for society overall” if** the argument shows *substantial, well-supported* harms that match these con conditions: (a) AI undermines critical thinking through an “authority/shortcut” dynamic that incentivizes users to accept lightly edited AI answers instead of evaluating claims, checking sources, and reasoning through uncertainty; (b) AI harms racial minorities by reproducing and amplifying racism, especially when deployed in high-impact settings like hiring, education, lending, or information exposure, producing discriminatory outcomes that fall disproportionately on racial minorities; (c) AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses; and/or (d) AI poses dangerous privacy risks.

**If both pro and con conditions are supported as substantial with no clear dominance after considering likelihood, scale/reach, and whether harms can be realistically mitigated (without merely assuming them away), treat the overall judgment as unresolved rather than concluding either side automatically.**

judgements.target_statement: For accessibility, speech-to-text, real-time captioning, screen-reader enhancements, and similar supports can be built into widely used consumer devices and applications, meaning they can reach many users without requiring extraordinary institutional buy-in.

judgements.reason: This directly denies the target statement’s claim that such supports can reach many users through widely used consumer devices and applications without extraordinary institutional buy-in.
